body.objective: Students will be able to accept and build offers in improvisation.
body.iCan: I can accept and build offers in improvisation.
successCriteria: I can accept offers from my scene partners
I can build on offers with "yes, and"
I can listen and respond in the moment
body.hook: Improvisers on stage have no script, no plan and no idea what their partner will say next, yet the best scenes look rehearsed. Their secret is two words: "Yes, and." Accept what your partner offers, then add something new.

vocabulary.definition: Acting without a script, making it up in the moment.
Anything a performer says or does that gives information in a scene.
Accepting an offer and adding new information.
Rejecting or ignoring an offer, which stops a scene.
Fully believing in and performing your choices.
Paying close attention so you can respond honestly.

study.title: Yes, And!
study.question: How does accepting offers build a scene?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. "Yes, but" vs "Yes, and" (10 minutes): In pairs, plan a class party. Round 1: every sentence starts with "Yes, but..." Round 2: every sentence starts with "Yes, and..." Which plan went further? Which felt better?
2. Gift giving (5 minutes): Partner A hands B an imaginary gift. B opens it and names it ("A pet snake!"). A accepts and adds ("I named him Gerald, and he loves jazz").
3. One-word story (10 minutes): In a circle, tell a story one word at a time. Keep it moving; accept every word.
4. Offer spotting (15 minutes): Pairs improvise a 1-minute scene from a starting line such as "Doctor, my elbow is glowing." The audience calls "Offer!" each time new information appears, and "Block!" if an offer is rejected.
Rule: in improv there are no wrong answers, only offers. Keep it safe and school-appropriate.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; "yes, and" is a widely used improvisation principle.
steps: Improvise scenes from a starting line

body.objective: Students will be able to create tableaux.
successCriteria: I can create a clear tableau with my group
I can use levels, facial expression and focus in a tableau
I can link tableaux to tell a story
body.hook: A news photo captures one frozen moment, yet tells a whole story. A tableau does the same thing on stage: a living picture made of still bodies that shows who, where and what is happening.

vocabulary.definition: A frozen picture created by performers' bodies.
High, middle and low positions in a scene.
Where the audience's attention is directed.
Moving smoothly from one tableau to the next.
When a performer in a tableau speaks their character's thoughts aloud.
The arrangement of bodies in the stage picture.

study.title: Living Pictures
study.question: How can frozen pictures tell a story?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Tableau rules (5 minutes): Freeze completely; use different levels (high, middle, low); show emotion on every face; face the audience (open body position); everyone's eyes or bodies should direct focus to the most important moment.
2. Quick tableaux (10 minutes): Groups of four get 30 seconds to make: a birthday party; the moment a goal is scored; a family photo gone wrong; discovering treasure.
3. Three-part story (20 minutes): Create three tableaux for a story: beginning, problem, ending. Ideas: a school field trip, a camping trip, a lost pet. Plan smooth transitions: on a count of eight, move slowly into the next picture.
4. Thought-tracking (10 minutes): When the teacher taps a performer's shoulder, they say one sentence their character is thinking.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: Which tableau told its story most clearly? Why?
How did levels make the pictures interesting?

study.product: Perform a three-tableau story with smooth transitions and thought-tracking, then explain how you directed focus.

body.objective: Students will be able to improvise a short scene with a beginning, middle and end.
body.iCan: I can improvise a short scene with a beginning, middle and end.
successCriteria: I can establish who, what and where early in a scene
I can build a scene to a problem and resolution
I can improvise a scene with a beginning, middle and end
body.hook: Even made-up scenes need a shape. A scene that just wanders feels pointless; one with a clear start, a problem and a change feels like a story. Today you combine "yes, and" with story structure.

vocabulary.definition: The characters, activity and setting of a scene.
The beginning of a scene that sets up the normal situation.
A problem or struggle in a scene.
How the problem is solved or how the scene ends.
Giving another character qualities through what you say.

study.title: Shape the Scene
study.question: How do improvisers create scenes with a clear shape?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Who, what, where (10 minutes): In pairs, start a scene and make the who, what and where clear within the first three lines without saying "We are..." Example: "Grandpa, your fishing line is tangled again." (who: grandchild and grandpa; what: fishing; where: lake or river.)
2. Endowment (5 minutes): Give your partner a quality with your words: "Coach, you've never lost a game." The partner accepts and plays it.
3. Structure (10 minutes): Learn the scene shape: platform (normal) → something changes (conflict) → it gets bigger → resolution.
4. Scenes (20 minutes): In pairs or threes, improvise 2-minute scenes from audience suggestions (a location and an object). The audience watches for: was the who, what, where clear? Was there a problem? Did it end?
5. Endings: Practise ending with a final line and a freeze, called out with "Scene!"
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Establish who, what and where in three lines
End with a final line and freeze
discussion: How quickly did your audience know the who, what and where?
How did the problem get bigger?
study.product: Improvise a two-minute scene with a clear platform, conflict and resolution, then write a short summary of its structure.
